Salary or Dividends? What Your Corporation's $100K Really Buys (2026)
yt.description:
Your company made $100,000. Salary or dividends? One puts about $5,800 more in your pocket.

All salary (Manitoba 2026, single owner): the company pays $95,354 + its half of CPP. After CPP ($9,293 in total) and income tax ($21,519), you keep $69,188.
All dividends: 9% corporate tax ($9,000), $91,000 paid out, $16,014 of personal tax. You keep $74,986.

So dividends win? The $5,798 bought something: salary put $9,293 into CPP (your future pension) and creates $17,164 of RRSP room (18% of earned income, up to the annual limit).

The twist: you don't have to pick one. You can mix both; the right mix depends on what you need now and later.
Own more than 40% of the voting shares? Your salary isn't insurable for EI. Plan the mix with an accountant.

Next: spousal RRSPs. How couples split retirement income.

Sources: Income Tax Act ss. 82(1)(b), 121, 146(1); Manitoba Income Tax Act s. 4.7; CPP Act ss. 12–13; EI Act s. 5(2)(b); CRA 2026 rates. Example only. General information, not tax advice.

$100K in your company: salary or dividends? 🇨🇦

Salary → keep $69,188 · $9,293 into CPP · $17,164 RRSP room
Dividends → keep $74,986 · no CPP · no RRSP room

The $5,798 isn't free money. It's what you give up for later.
You can mix both. Own >40% of the voting shares? No EI on your salary.
